note: Subjects/9702 Physics/10 D.C. circuits/10.1 Practical circuits.md
outline: Use standard symbols to draw complete conducting loops. Put an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across a component. Source e.m.f. $E=W/Q$ is energy supplied per unit charge around the complete circuit. P.d. is energy transferred from electrical energy per unit charge across a component. With internal resistance $r$, terminal p.d. is $V=E-Ir$; increasing current increases lost volts.

misconceptions.refutation: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points, so connect it across the component.
misconceptions.contrast: An ammeter is connected in series.

misconceptions.statement: A wire crossing always makes a junction.
misconceptions.refutation: Only a marked junction joins branches; a crossing without a junction is not a connection.
misconceptions.contrast: Trace each continuous path between junctions.

misconceptions.statement: E.m.f. is the energy delivered only to the external resistor per charge.
misconceptions.refutation: E.m.f. is energy supplied per unit charge to the complete circuit, including internal resistance.
misconceptions.contrast: Terminal p.d. describes energy per charge available externally.

misconceptions.statement: E.m.f. and p.d. are both total energy.
misconceptions.refutation: Each is energy per unit charge: e.m.f. is energy supplied by the source; p.d. is energy transferred from electrical energy in a component.

misconceptions.statement: Terminal p.d. stays equal to e.m.f. as current rises.
misconceptions.refutation: The internal drop $Ir$ grows, so terminal p.d. $V=E-Ir$ falls.
misconceptions.contrast: At zero current the lost volts are zero.

items.examiner: Candidates found this question difficult, with many selecting C or D rather than the correct answer A. If the 10 Ω fixed resistor is replaced by a resistor of resistance 20 Ω, the current I in the resistor will fall. The power dissipated in the fixed resistor is I2R when its resistance is R. The value of R has doubled but I has approximately halved, so the power dissipated in the fixed resistor must decrease (i.e. statement C is correct). flashcards.back: One long and one short parallel line.
A rectangle in the conducting path.
Energy transferred per unit charge by a source in driving charge around a complete circuit.

9702-10.1.1.motivate: Circuit symbols let any reader identify components without seeing the apparatus.
9702-10.1.1.establish: Recall and use the standard circuit symbols in section 6 of the syllabus. A cell has a long and short parallel line; several pairs form a battery. A fixed resistor is a rectangle; a variable resistor has a diagonal arrow. A lamp has a cross in a circle, an ammeter A in a circle, and a voltmeter V in a circle. Recognise the standard forms for an open or closed switch, diode, light-dependent resistor, thermistor and oscilloscope. Preserve polarity where the symbol gives it.
9702-10.1.1.connect: Once each symbol is recognisable, follow the wires and junctions to interpret the circuit.
9702-10.1.1.note:
- Use the section 6 symbols consistently.
- A cell is one long and one short line.
- A and V inside circles denote meters.
9702-10.1.1.self_explain: How would you distinguish a cell from a battery and a fixed from a variable resistor?

9702-10.1.2.motivate: A circuit picture tells you which parts share a current or a potential difference.
9702-10.1.2.establish: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using the section 6 symbols. Trace continuous conducting paths and mark junctions clearly. A crossing without a junction is not an electrical connection. Series components lie on one path and share current; parallel components connect between the same two junctions and share p.d. Put an ammeter in series with the component whose current is needed. Put a voltmeter across the two points whose p.d. is needed. An open switch breaks its path.
9702-10.1.2.connect: Correctly locating a voltmeter across the source lets you identify terminal p.d.
9702-10.1.2.note:
- Trace wires through marked junctions.
- Ammeter: series.
- Voltmeter: across two points.
- Open switch: broken path.
9702-10.1.2.self_explain: Where would you place meters to measure current through and p.d. across a lamp?

9702-10.1.3.motivate: A voltage rating tells how much energy a source supplies to each coulomb.
9702-10.1.3.establish: Define the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source as energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit. In symbols, $E=W/Q$, where $W$ is energy supplied to charge $Q$. Thus $W=EQ$. The volt is one joule per coulomb. The energy supplied by the source includes energy subsequently dissipated inside the source as well as in the external circuit.
9702-10.1.3.connect: Compare that total supply per charge with the energy transferred per charge across one component.
9702-10.1.3.note:
- $E=W/Q$: energy per unit charge.
- The charge goes around a complete circuit.
- Unit: $\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ or V.
9702-10.1.3.self_explain: What does a 9.0 V label tell you about energy supplied to each coulomb?

9702-10.1.4.motivate: Equal numbers in volts can describe different stages of the energy journey.
9702-10.1.4.establish: Distinguish e.m.f. from potential difference by energy transfer. E.m.f. is energy supplied by the source per unit charge around the complete circuit, often from chemical to electrical energy. P.d. across a component is energy transferred from electrical energy to other forms per unit charge in that component. A resistor transfers it mainly to thermal energy; a lamp transfers it to light and thermal energy. Both are measured in volts, or joules per coulomb. Terminal p.d. measures the energy per charge available to the external circuit.
9702-10.1.4.connect: Internal resistance explains why terminal p.d. can be below source e.m.f.
9702-10.1.4.note:
- E.m.f.: supplied energy per charge.
- P.d.: transferred energy per charge.
- Both use volts.
9702-10.1.4.self_explain: Why can e.m.f. and resistor p.d. have the same value yet describe different transfers?

9702-10.1.5.motivate: A source can read less across its terminals while delivering current.
9702-10.1.5.establish: A real source has internal resistance $r$. Current $I$ produces an internal p.d. $Ir$ called lost volts. For a discharging source, $E=V+Ir$, so terminal p.d. $V=E-Ir$. Increasing current at fixed e.m.f. and internal resistance raises the internal energy dissipated per unit charge and lowers terminal p.d. At zero current, the lost volts are zero and $V=E$. Raising external resistance usually lowers current, so terminal p.d. rises towards e.m.f. A voltmeter across the source terminals reads $V$.
9702-10.1.5.connect: This relationship prepares you to apply circuit laws to complete loops and networks.
9702-10.1.5.note:
- Lost volts across internal resistance: $Ir$.
- Terminal p.d.: $V=E-Ir$.
- At $I=0$, $V=E$.
9702-10.1.5.self_explain: Why does adding a parallel load often lower the voltmeter reading across a real cell?
